### Imports

One `justfile` can include the contents of another using `import` statements.

If you have the following `justfile`:

```justfile
import 'foo/bar.just'

a: b
  @echo A
```

And the following text in `foo/bar.just`:

```just
b:
  @echo B
```

`foo/bar.just` will be included in `justfile` and recipe `b` will be defined:

```console
$ just b
B
$ just a
B
A
```

The `import` path can be absolute or relative to the location of the justfile
containing it. A leading `~/` in the import path is replaced with the current
user's home directory.

Justfiles are insensitive to order, so included files can reference variables
and recipes defined after the `import` statement.

Imported files can themselves contain `import`s, which are processed
recursively.

`allow-duplicate-recipes` and `allow-duplicate-variables` allow duplicate
recipes and variables, respectively, to override each other, instead of
producing an error.

Within a module, later definitions override earlier definitions:

```just
set allow-duplicate-recipes

foo:

foo:
  echo 'yes'
```

When `import`s are involved, things unfortunately get much more complicated and
hard to explain.

Shallower definitions always override deeper definitions, so recipes at the top
level will override recipes in imports, and recipes in an import will override
recipes in an import which itself imports those recipes.

When two duplicate definitions are imported and are at the same depth, the one
from the earlier import will override the one from the later import.

This is because `just` uses a stack when processing imports, pushing imports
onto the stack in source-order, and always processing the top of the stack
next, so earlier imports are actually handled later by the compiler.

This is definitely a bug, but since `just` has very strong backwards
compatibility guarantees and we take enormous pains not to break anyone's
`justfile`, see issue [#2540](https://github.com/casey/just/issues/2540) for
discussion on whether or not we can actually fix it.

Imports may be made optional by putting a `?` after the `import` keyword:

```just
import? 'foo/bar.just'
```

Importing the same source file multiple times is not an error<sup>1.37.0</sup>.
This allows importing multiple justfiles, for example `foo.just` and
`bar.just`, which both import a third justfile containing shared recipes, for
example `baz.just`, without the duplicate import of `baz.just` being an error:

```justfile
# justfile
import 'foo.just'
import 'bar.just'
```

```justfile
# foo.just
import 'baz.just'
foo: baz
```

```justfile
# bar.just
import 'baz.just'
bar: baz
```

```just
# baz
baz:
```

### Modules

A `justfile` can declare modules using `mod` statements<sup>1.19.0</sup>.

`mod` statements were stabilized in `just`<sup>1.31.0</sup>.

If you have the following `justfile`:

```justfile
mod bar

a:
  @echo A
```

And the following text in `bar.just`:

```just
b:
  @echo B
```

`bar.just` will be included in `justfile` as a submodule. Recipes, aliases, and
variables defined in one submodule cannot be used in another, and each module
uses its own settings.

Recipes in submodules can be invoked as subcommands:

```console
$ just bar b
B
```

Or with path syntax:

```console
$ just bar::b
B
```

If a module is named `foo`, `just` will search for the module file in `foo.just`,
`foo/mod.just`, `foo/justfile`, and `foo/.justfile`. In the latter two cases,
the module file may have any capitalization.

Module statements may be of the form:

```justfile
mod foo 'PATH'
```

Which loads the module's source file from `PATH`, instead of from the usual
locations. A leading `~/` in `PATH` is replaced with the current user's home
directory. `PATH` may point to the module source file itself, or to a directory
containing the module source file with the name `mod.just`, `justfile`, or
`.justfile`. In the latter two cases, the module file may have any
capitalization.

Environment files are loaded for each module, respecting that module's related
settings. Environment variables from parent modules are visible in child
modules.

Recipes in submodules without the `[no-cd]` attribute run with the working
directory set to the directory containing the submodule source file.

`justfile()` and `justfile_directory()` always return the path to the root
justfile and the directory that contains it, even when called from submodule
recipes.

Modules may be made optional by putting a `?` after the `mod` keyword:

```just
mod? foo
```

Missing source files for optional modules do not produce an error. If a recipe
or alias depends on a missing optional module, directly, or transitively, it
will be disabled. Attempting to invoke a disabled recipe or alias is an error,
but other non-disabled recipes can still be run.<sup>1.52.0</sup>

Optional modules with no source file do not conflict, so you can have multiple
mod statements with the same name, but with different source file paths, as
long as at most one source file exists:

```just
mod? foo 'bar.just'
mod? foo 'baz.just'
```

Modules may be given doc comments which appear in `--list`
output<sup>1.30.0</sup>:

```justfile
# foo is a great module!
mod foo
```

```console
$ just --list
Available recipes:
    foo ... # foo is a great module!
```

Modules are still missing a lot of features, for example, the ability to refer
to variables in other modules. See the [module improvement tracking
issue](https://github.com/casey/just/issues/2252) for more information.

### Invoking `justfile`s in Other Directories

If the first argument passed to `just` contains a `/`, then the following
occurs:

1.  The argument is split at the last `/`.

2.  The part before the last `/` is treated as a directory. `just` will start
    its search for the `justfile` there, instead of in the current directory.

3.  The part after the last slash is treated as a normal argument, or ignored
    if it is empty.

This may seem a little strange, but it's useful if you wish to run a command in
a `justfile` that is in a subdirectory.

For example, if you are in a directory which contains a subdirectory named
`foo`, which contains a `justfile` with the recipe `build`, which is also the
default recipe, the following are all equivalent:

```console
$ (cd foo && just build)
$ just foo/build
$ just foo/
```

Additional recipes after the first are sought in the same `justfile`. For
example, the following are both equivalent:

```console
$ just foo/a b
$ (cd foo && just a b)
```

And will both invoke recipes `a` and `b` in `foo/justfile`.

### Fallback to parent `justfile`s

If a recipe is not found in a `justfile` and the `fallback` setting is set,
`just` will look for `justfile`s in the parent directory and up, until it
reaches the root directory. `just` will stop after it reaches a `justfile` in
which the `fallback` setting is `false` or unset.

As an example, suppose the current directory contains this `justfile`:

```just
set fallback
foo:
  echo foo
```

And the parent directory contains this `justfile`:

```just
bar:
  echo bar
```

```console
$ just bar
Trying ../justfile
echo bar
bar
```

### Global Fallback Justfile

A global fallback justfile may be set with `--global-fallback-justfile <PATH>`,
or by setting the `JUST_GLOBAL_FALLBACK_JUSTFILE` environment variable.

If no justfile is found, or if the search for a fallback does not succeed, the
global fallback justfile is used instead. The working directory is set to the
root of the current project, as determined by the presence of a directory like
`.git`, or the invocation directory if no such directory is found. The global
fallback justfile may itself use `set fallback`.

The global fallback justfile is ignored when `--justfile`, `--global-justfile`,
or `--working-directory` is passed.

content.text:
**1. Multiple justfiles in one `just -l`: yes, but you have to declare them.** `just` only loads one root `justfile` from the current directory or the nearest parent. It doesn't auto-discover sibling files. The root file can pull in others in two ways:

- **`import 'foo.just'`** merges the file's recipes into the root list, so they show up in `just -l` with no prefix. Imports can nest, and `import?` makes one optional. If two files define the same recipe name it's an error, unless you turn on `set allow-duplicate-recipes` (#2).
- **`mod foo`** (or `mod foo 'path'`) loads the file as a namespace, so you call `just foo recipe` or `just foo::recipe`. Plain `just -l` only shows `foo ...`. To see every recipe, use `just -l --list-submodules` or set `JUST_LIST_SUBMODULES=true` (#2, #3).

There are also flags that point `just` at other files without merging anything: `-f`, `--justfile-name`, `set fallback` (if a recipe isn't found, look in parent justfiles), `--global-fallback-justfile`, and `just dir/recipe`. None of these combine everything into one list (#2, #3).

I checked all of this with your installed `just 1.59.0` in a temp folder: an imported recipe and a module recipe both listed and ran (#3).

**2. Merging a Makefile: no.** `just` doesn't read Makefiles at all. I put a folder containing only a Makefile under the test justfile, and `just -l` just went up to the parent justfile. None of the Makefile's targets appeared (#3). The README only mentions `make` when comparing the two tools.

The workaround is to call `make` from a recipe. Either:
- forward everything: `make *args:` with the command `make {{args}}`, which I tested and `just make mk` worked (#3); or
- write one small recipe per target (`build:` running `make build`) so each target shows up separately in `just -l`.

**What this means for the feature:** each project would have one root `justfile` that `import`s the shared or local `.just` files and wraps any Makefile targets. A doc comment above each recipe shows up as its description in `just -l` (#3). The agent then only needs `just -l` to see what's available and `just <recipe>` to run it. `--dump --dump-format json` gives the recipe list in a form a program can read, if the YAML side needs it.

# Design: project context and prompt-cache placement

> Status: **implemented** (see "Implementation notes").
> Based on pi `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` 1.0.4
> (`system-prompt.js`, `extensions.md`, the Anthropic provider) and the `cpa` provider in
> `config/models.json`.

## Goal

Give each run its project's rules, commands, workflows and docs, written by the user in one
manifest (`project.yaml`) and loaded by a pi extension, while keeping the prompt cache
effective:

- The system prompt, append prompt and skills stay byte-stable, so their cached prefix is reused
  across projects.
- Project content sits after them, stable for the whole session.
- The conversation only ever grows by appending.

Out of scope for now:

- How the project folder gets mounted was left open here; it is now set up in OpenShell as a
  read-only Docker volume mount (`openshell/README.md`, "Project folder").
- **Memory.** No memory store and no tool for the agent to save anything. All project context
  is written by the user; the agent only reads it. Memory may be designed later (see "Future").

## Cache background

- Anthropic caches by **exact prefix** over `tools → system → messages`. A cache marker stores
  the prefix up to that point; a later request reuses it if its own prefix is byte-identical.
- At most **4 markers** per request. A lookup checks about **20 blocks** back from each marker.
- Minimum cacheable size about 1–4k tokens (model-dependent). Lifetime 5 minutes, refreshed on
  every hit.
- Caches are separate per organization/API key, so all requests must reach the same upstream
  account. Today that holds: `cpa` has session affinity on and a single Claude account.
- pi sends a request on **every turn** (after each batch of tool calls), not only per user
  message. Within a run, gaps are usually seconds, so the 5-minute lifetime rarely expires.
- With `cpa` pricing (Sonnet 5.5: input $2/M, cache write $2.5/M, cache read $0.2/M), a cold
  start of a ~5k shared prefix costs about $0.01. On long runs the cost is dominated by
  re-reading the whole context each turn, so **context size matters more than prefix sharing**.

....
Not a problem for now, and the design stays as is: it is built for a future API-key plan, where
the proxy does not cloak and the layout above is sent unchanged. (`"prompt_cache_options":
{"mode": "explicit"}` makes the proxy keep our markers even when cloaking.)

## Scenarios and projects

A scenario chooses the system prompt and the skills (plus its tools and result schema). A project
chooses rules, commands, workflows and docs. Neither refers to the other: `project.yaml` has no
scenario-specific sections.

## The project folder

```
/project/                      mounted read-only; the agent cannot change its own instructions
  project.yaml
  workflows/release.md
  workflows/payments-change.md
  docs/architecture.md
```

The workspace (code) is the cwd, `/sandbox`. Paths in `project.yaml` are relative to the folder
that contains it. The mount path appears in block B, so it must be the same on every run.

### `project.yaml`

```yaml
version: 1
name: billing-service
description: Payment and invoicing backend (Node 22, Postgres).

# Short, always-on rules, in this order.
rules:
  - Never commit to main; work on the current branch.
  - Do not add dependencies without saying why in the result.

# One-line invocations only; anything with more than one step is a workflow.
# Key = the exact command (quote it if it contains ": "), value = what it does.
commands:
  npm ci: Install dependencies from the lockfile.
  npm test: Run all unit tests.
  npm test -- --grep <pattern>: Run only the tests matching a pattern.

# General-purpose CLI tools the agent may use. Key = executable name, value = what it is for.
# The agent learns each one from its own help (`<tool> docs`, `<tool> skill`, `<tool> -h`).
cli_tools:
  synotool: Synology internal tooling (chat, deploy).

# Strictly step-by-step instructions for one specific task. Index only; read on demand.
# Guidance for one area of the code is a workflow too.
workflows:
  - path: workflows/release.md
    when: Cutting a release or bumping the version.
  - path: workflows/payments-change.md
    when: Changing anything under src/payments/.

# Reference material. Index only; read on demand.
docs:
  - path: docs/architecture.md
    when: Before changing module boundaries or adding a service.
```

`when` is written as a trigger: the condition under which the agent should read the file.

### `AGENTS.md`

Not part of the manifest. The extension reads `AGENTS.md` at the root of the workspace (cwd) if
it exists, and includes it in full. Only that one file: no parent folders, no subfolders, no
`CLAUDE.md`. It is read once at session start; edits the agent makes to it during the run show up
in the next session. It is included with or without a project manifest.

pi's own context-file loading stays off (`-na`), because it would place the file before skills
and also pick up parent folders.

In personal pi (the extension is in the package manifest) pi's context files may be on. With
`--project`, `before_agent_start` empties `systemPromptOptions.contextFiles` on every prompt, the
same effect as `-nc`. Without `--project`, if pi loaded any context files, the extension adds no
sections and skips the cache split, leaving pi's behavior unchanged.

### Rendering

Block B is a set of extension sections after `<cwd>`, in this order; pi wraps each in a tag of
the same name. Names are prefixed so they can't collide with pi's own sections (`rules`, `docs`).

```
<project>
name: billing-service
Payment and invoicing backend (Node 22, Postgres).
</project>

<project_rules>
- Never commit to main; work on the current branch.
- Do not add dependencies without saying why in the result.
</project_rules>

<agents_md>
path: /sandbox/AGENTS.md
…file content…
</agents_md>

<project_commands>
Run from /sandbox:
- `npm ci`: Install dependencies from the lockfile.
- `npm test`: Run all unit tests.
- `npm test -- --grep <pattern>`: Run only the tests matching a pattern.
</project_commands>

<project_cli_tools>
General-purpose CLI tools. Before using one, learn it from its own help: run `<tool> docs`, `<tool> skill` or `<tool> -h` (whichever it supports; subcommands may have their own) and follow it:
- `synotool`: Synology internal tooling (chat, deploy).
</project_cli_tools>

<project_workflows>
Before doing one of these tasks, read its file and follow the steps in order. If several apply, follow them one after another, finishing each before starting the next:
- /project/workflows/release.md: Cutting a release or bumping the version.
- /project/workflows/payments-change.md: Changing anything under src/payments/.
</project_workflows>

<project_docs>
Read every doc whose condition applies; a task can need several docs on different topics:
- /project/docs/architecture.md: Before changing module boundaries or adding a service.
</project_docs>
```

Rules for byte-identical output:

- Keep the manifest's order everywhere (lists and `commands` keys); never sort.
- Line endings become `\n`, trailing whitespace is trimmed, file content ends with exactly one
  newline. File content is otherwise included as written.
- No generated values in the text: no timestamps, sizes, hashes or counts.
- Empty or missing sections are left out.
- `report.json` records a hash of the rendered block B, so a changed prefix between runs of the
  same project is visible.

### Validation

TypeBox schema, strict:

- `version: 1`; `name` required; `description`, `rules`, `commands`, `cli_tools`, `workflows`,
  `docs` optional.
- Unknown keys are errors (a typo must not silently do nothing).
- Command keys and descriptions are single lines; `cli_tools` keys are one word (an executable).
- Every `workflows`/`docs` path must exist inside the project folder; no file listed twice.
- Warning (not error) when block B is over about 8k tokens: it is paid on every turn.

### Wiring

- Order: `pi-agent run --project <dir>`, then `PI_AGENT_PROJECT` (when that folder has a
  `project.yaml`), then the `project` entry in settings.json (see "Project source").
- Image: `docker/pi-agent.sh` defaults `PI_AGENT_PROJECT=/project`. Locally there is no default.
- The wrapper validates the manifest before starting pi and passes the folder to the extension
  with a pi flag.

## Decisions

- **Manifest only.** Project context comes only from `project.yaml`; nothing is discovered by
  scanning folders. The project owner keeps the manifest up to date. The one fixed exception is
  `AGENTS.md` at the workspace root.
- **No scoped instructions.** Nothing is attached to tool results; area-specific guidance is a
  workflow.
- **Commands are one-liners** with a description; multi-step procedures are workflows.
- **Scenarios** choose the system prompt and skills only; projects don't vary by scenario.
- **Cache retention: 5 minutes** (pi's default). No 1-hour option planned.
- **No memory** for now.

## Future: memory

Not designed yet. The layout leaves room for it without changing the cache rules: a memory index
would go into block B as a snapshot taken at session start (like the docs index), and anything
saved during a run would only show up in the next session. Whether the agent may write memory
at all, and with what review, is part of that later design.

Good idea, and pi supports it well. Before I build it, there are a few pi limits that change the design, and a few decisions I need from you.

### Things that change the plan

1. **Repeating `--tag` won't work.** pi stores extension flags in a `Map`, so `--tag a --tag b` keeps only `b` (#44). Extension flags can only be `string` or `boolean` (#44). Options:
   - **comma-separated only:** `--tag a,b`, the same format as `/tags`. This is simple and consistent; I recommend it.
   - read `process.argv` ourselves to collect repeated flags. That's fragile because it goes around pi's parser.
2. **Use a `custom` entry, not a `custom_message`.** `pi.appendEntry()` writes data to the session file that the model never sees (#43). A `custom_message` goes into the model's context, which costs tokens and changes the cached prompt. Tags are metadata, so `custom` fits. The metrics extension already works this way.
3. **"Override" should mean appending a new entry each time.** The session file is append-only, so each change adds `{ tags: [...] }` with the full list, and the last entry wins. This also gives you a history of tag changes.
4. **`/tags` will be a command, not a tool.** In pi a "tool" is something the model calls. I assume tags belong to you and the model shouldn't change them, so `/tags` would be a slash command only.

### Decisions I need from you

- **Resuming with `--tag`:** if you run `pi -c --tag x`, should it replace the session's tags? My suggestion: replace them, but only write a new entry if the list actually changed, so resuming doesn't pile up duplicates.
- **Forks and branches:** should tags belong to the whole session file (last entry in the file) or to each branch? Whole session is simpler and matches "metadata of this session".
- **Normalization:** I'd trim spaces, drop empty items, remove duplicates and keep your order. Do you also want lowercasing or a character limit like `[A-Za-z0-9._:/-]`? A limit keeps tags usable as filters later.
- **Key/value tags:** should tags like `ticket:ABC-123` or `env:prod` have meaning? That costs nothing now and makes later filtering much better.
- **`/tags` usage:**
  - `/tags a,b` sets the list.
  - `/tags` with no arguments shows the current tags.
  - Clearing needs its own syntax, such as `/tags --clear` or `/tags -`.

### Worth adding

- **Where tags show up:**
  - in the footer status, so you can see the current tags;
  - in the startup notice (the activation-hint extension already announces the scenario and project).
- **Autocomplete** for `/tags` from tags you used before.
- **Sandbox runs:** a `tags` field in `task.json`, passed to pi as `--tag`, and written to `report.json`. Without this, tags only work in interactive pi.
- **Session upload:** send the current tags with the upload (as a header or a small metadata field), so the server can index them without reading the whole file.
- **A shared reader**, like `currentTags(entries)` in `src/shared/`, used by the wrapper, the upload and any later tooling, so nobody re-parses the file their own way.
- **Packaging:** add the new extension to the package manifest and to the wrapper's bundled extensions. Sandbox runs start pi with `-ne`, so it won't load there otherwise.

If you agree with comma-only `--tag`, a `custom` entry where the last one in the file wins, and `/tags` to show / `/tags a,b` to set / `/tags --clear` to clear, tell me which of the "worth adding" items you want and I'll build it.

Session tags are built and committed in three parts, and `npm run check` passes with all 250 tests (#60). The tests use a stand-in for pi; I haven't run the real pi with `--tags` or `/tags`, so the footer and autocomplete haven't been seen in the actual TUI yet.

**Commits** (#63):
1. `a1f9466` **Shared reader**, `src/shared/tags.ts`: `parseTags` and `normalizeTags` handle input, and `currentTags`, `tagHistory` and `sessionFileTags` read tags back from session entries or a raw `.jsonl` file (#48, #49).
2. `276bcbb` **The extension**, `src/tags/`: the `--tags` flag, the `/tags` command, the footer and autocomplete. It's in the package manifest and bundled as `dist/tags.js` (#55).
3. `73dc2ca` **Sandbox runs**: `task.json` takes `"tags": ["bug","ui"]` and the wrapper passes them to pi as `--tags bug,ui`. They're written to the session file only, not `report.json` (#63).

**How it behaves:**
- **Format:** tags are lowercased and limited to `a-z 0-9 . _ : / -`, up to 64 characters each. Spaces, empty items and duplicates are dropped, and your order is kept.
- **Session file:** each change adds a `pi-agent.tags` entry holding the whole list, `{ "version": 1, "tags": [...], "source": "flag" | "command" }`. The last entry in the file is the session's tags. Nothing is written when the list doesn't change.
- **`--tags` at startup** replaces the session's tags, including when resuming with `-c`, `--session` or `--fork`. pi reports all of these as a normal startup, so the flag applies to them (#61, #62).
- **`/new`, `/resume`, `/fork` and `/reload` ignore `--tags`.** Otherwise a reload would undo whatever you set with `/tags`.
- **`/tags`** shows the tags, `/tags a,b` replaces them and `/tags --clear` clears them. Invalid input shows an error and changes nothing.
- **An invalid `--tags`** writes an error entry and stops pi, like the other extensions' startup errors. In `task.json` it fails the run as invalid input (exit 2).
- **Autocomplete** suggests tags used in this session and in the other sessions in the same folder (the 200 newest files), and completes the part after the last comma.
- **Footer** shows `tags: a,b`.
- **Resumed sandbox runs:** a task without `tags` keeps the previous session's tags; a task with `tags` replaces them.

On your server, `sessionFileTags(text)` from `src/shared/tags.ts` returns the uploaded file's tags. The README has a new "Session tags" section and the `tags` field in the task-file example.

The tags now appear at the start of the cwd line, in the same grey as the rest of the footer. This is committed as `b607ad9` (#77), and all 252 tests pass (#75). I haven't looked at it in a live pi session yet, only in tests.

```
[bug,ui] ~/Project/pi-agent (main)
```

**Color:** I rendered a sample line, and the tags and the cwd use exactly the same grey (#76). A test checks this, so it will catch it if they ever differ.

**How it works:** pi gives extensions no way to add text to its cwd line. Text from `setStatus` always goes on a separate line below, which is why the tags were on their own line and in white. To fix that, I replaced the footer with a copy of pi's own footer that has the tags added in front of the cwd. pi doesn't hand its existing footer to extensions, so the copy is built from the session information extensions can see.

This has some side effects:
- **Only while tags exist:** the replacement footer is used only when the session has tags. `/tags --clear` puts pi's normal footer back.
- **One detail is missing:** if you use a model that routes each request to another model, the footer won't show where requests went. The rest of the footer looks the same as before.
- **Other footer extensions:** if another extension also replaces the footer, whichever one sets it last wins.
- **pi upgrades:** this depends on how pi's footer works internally, which could change in a pi update. The footer test would most likely catch that.
- **RPC mode:** I left the old separate tags line there, since RPC has no footer to change.

`dist/scenario-profile.js` still has its earlier uncommitted change, and nothing is pushed.
